concepts.name: SQLite WAL checkpointing
concepts.reason: It is the target concept and covers transferring WAL content, checkpoint progress, reset, modes, and failure behavior.

concepts.name: Automatic checkpointing
concepts.reason: It governs when SQLite starts automatic checkpoints and how the application can configure them.

concepts.name: Reader end marks and checkpoint progress
concepts.reason: Reader end marks limit safe checkpoint progress, and the checkpoint can resume from its recorded position.

concepts.name: Checkpoint modes
concepts.reason: The modes differ in whether they wait, block writers, restart the WAL, or truncate it.

concepts.name: Checkpoint sync ordering
concepts.reason: Sync ordering protects database integrity when a checkpoint transfers WAL content and resets the log.

concepts.name: Checkpoint read and write performance
concepts.reason: Checkpoint frequency trades smaller WAL files and faster reads against amortized write costs.

concepts.name: Checkpoint locks and busy handlers
concepts.reason: Lock acquisition and busy-handler behavior determine how checkpoint attempts respond to contention.

concepts.name: Checkpoint starvation
concepts.reason: Persistent readers can prevent checkpoint completion and allow the WAL to grow without bound.

concepts.name: WAL rewind and reuse
concepts.reason: A completed and synced checkpoint can let a writer reuse the WAL from its beginning.

concepts.name: Large write transaction effects
concepts.reason: A write transaction can prevent WAL reset and cause a large log before checkpointing can finish.

concepts.name: Transaction WAL footprint across versions
concepts.reason: The packet documents a SQLite 3.11.0 change to WAL size behavior for a single transaction.

concepts.name: WAL reader and writer concurrency beyond checkpoint behavior
concepts.reason: Its broader concurrency behavior is outside the checkpointing boundary and belongs in a separate handoff.

concepts.name: WAL activation and shared-memory requirements
concepts.reason: Mode activation and VFS requirements are outside the checkpointing boundary and belong in a separate handoff.

claims.text: A checkpoint transfers transactions from the WAL file back into the original database.
claims.quote: Moving the WAL file transactions back into the database is called a " checkpoint ".

claims.text: When all WAL content is transferred and synced and no readers use the WAL, a writer rewinds it to the beginning.
claims.quote: if the entire WAL has been transferred into the database and synced and if no readers are making use of the WAL, then the writer will rewind the WAL back to the beginning

claims.text: Each new database connection defaults to automatic checkpointing at a threshold of 1000 pages, or the compile-time default.
claims.quote: Every new database connection defaults to having the auto-checkpoint enabled with a threshold of 1000 or SQLITE_DEFAULT_WAL_AUTOCHECKPOINT pages.

claims.text: Checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() and by the automatic checkpoint mechanism use PASSIVE mode.
claims.quote: All checkpoints initiated by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint() and by the automatic checkpoint mechanism are PASSIVE.

claims.text: A checkpoint may run with readers but must stop before a WAL page past any current reader's end mark.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can run concurrently with readers, however the checkpoint must stop when it reaches a page in the WAL that is past the end mark of any current reader.

claims.text: The checkpoint records its progress in the wal-index and resumes from that position on a later invocation.
claims.quote: The checkpoint remembers (in the wal-index) how far it got and will resume transferring content from the WAL to the database from where it left off on the next invocation.

claims.text: Read performance deteriorates as the WAL grows because each reader must check the WAL for content.
claims.quote: read performance deteriorates as the WAL file grows in size since each reader must check the WAL file for the content

claims.text: Checkpoint sync operations help avoid database corruption after power loss or a hard reboot.
claims.quote: Checkpointing does require sync operations in order to avoid the possibility of database corruption following a power loss or hard reboot.

claims.text: A reader's end mark stays unchanged for the transaction, so its read sees a single database point in time.
claims.quote: for any particular reader, the end mark is unchanged for the duration of the transaction, thus ensuring that a single read transaction only sees the database content as it existed at a single point in time.

claims.text: A long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.
claims.quote: Thus a long-running read transaction can prevent a checkpointer from making progress.

claims.text: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage before its content is transferred into the database.
claims.quote: The WAL must be synced to persistent storage prior to moving content from the WAL into the database

claims.text: The database file must be synced before the WAL is reset.
claims.quote: and the database file must be synced prior to resetting the WAL.

claims.text: The checkpointer transfers pages in ascending order to make as many database writes sequential as possible.
claims.quote: The checkpointer makes an effort to do as many sequential page writes to the database as it can (the pages are transferred from WAL to database in ascending order)

claims.text: Frequent checkpoints keep the WAL small to maximize read performance.
claims.quote: To maximize the read performance, one wants to keep the WAL as small as possible and hence run checkpoints frequently, perhaps as often as every COMMIT.

claims.text: Infrequent checkpoints amortize checkpoint cost across more writes to maximize write performance.
claims.quote: To maximize write performance, one wants to amortize the cost of each checkpoint over as many writes as possible, meaning that one wants to run checkpoints infrequently and let the WAL grow as large as possible before each checkpoint.

claims.text: The default checkpoint runs in the COMMIT thread that crosses the size limit, making most commits fast but occasional checkpointing commits slower.
claims.quote: This has the effect of causing most COMMIT operations to be very fast but an occasional COMMIT (those that trigger a checkpoint) to be much slower.

claims.text: sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2 supports PASSIVE, FULL, RESTART, TRUNCATE, and NOOP modes.
claims.quote: The M parameter must be a valid checkpoint mode : SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_NOOP

claims.text: NOOP checkpoints zero frames and can read the log and checkpoint counts through output parameters.
claims.quote: This mode always checkpoints zero frames. The only reason to invoke a NOOP checkpoint is to access the values returned by sqlite3_wal_checkpoint_v2() via output parameters *pnLog and *pnCkpt.

claims.text: PASSIVE attempts to checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for readers or writers.
claims.quote: Checkpoint as many frames as possible without waiting for any database readers or writers to finish, then sync the database file if all frames in the log were checkpointed.

claims.text: PASSIVE can leave the checkpoint unfinished when readers or writers are concurrent.
claims.quote: On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished if there are concurrent readers or writers.

claims.text: PASSIVE never invokes the busy-handler callback.
claims.quote: The busy-handler callback is never invoked in the SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE mode. On the other hand, passive mode might leave the checkpoint unfinished if there are concurrent readers or writers.

claims.text: FULL waits until there is no writer and all readers use the latest snapshot, then checkpoints all log frames and syncs the database.
claims.quote: This mode blocks (it invokes the busy-handler callback ) until there is no database writer and all readers are reading from the most recent database snapshot. It then checkpoints all frames in the log file and syncs the database file.

claims.text: FULL blocks new database writers while pending but allows new readers to continue unimpeded.
claims.quote: This mode blocks new database writers while it is pending, but new database readers are allowed to continue unimpeded.

claims.text: RESTART waits until all readers use only the database file, ensuring the next writer restarts the log from the beginning.
claims.quote: it blocks (calls the busy-handler callback ) until all readers are reading from the database file only. This ensures that the next writer will restart the log file from the beginning.

claims.text: TRUNCATE adds truncation of the log file to zero bytes before successful return.
claims.quote: This mode works the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART with the addition that it also truncates the log file to zero bytes just prior to a successful return.

claims.text: If another process is checkpointing, an exclusive checkpoint-lock conflict returns SQLITE_BUSY.
claims.quote: All calls obtain an exclusive "checkpoint" lock on the database file. If any other process is running a checkpoint operation at the same time, the lock cannot be obtained and SQLITE_BUSY is returned.

claims.text: FULL, RESTART, and TRUNCATE obtain the writer lock and use a configured busy handler to retry delayed lock acquisition.
claims.quote: The SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_FULL, RESTART and TRUNCATE modes also obtain the exclusive "writer" lock on the database file. If the writer lock cannot be obtained immediately, and a busy-handler is configured, it is invoked and the writer lock retried

claims.text: If the busy handler returns zero while waiting for the writer lock or readers, the checkpoint proceeds in PASSIVE fashion without further blocking.
claims.quote: If the busy-handler returns 0 before the writer lock is obtained or while waiting for database readers, the checkpoint operation proceeds from that point in the same way as SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_PASSIVE - checkpointing as many frames as possible without blocking any further

claims.text: Passing zero or a negative value for the auto-checkpoint threshold disables automatic checkpoints.
claims.quote: Passing zero or a negative value as the N parameter disables automatic checkpoints entirely.

claims.text: Disabling automatic checkpointing removes the safeguard against excessive WAL growth.
claims.quote: If an application disables the automatic checkpoint, then there is nothing to prevent the WAL file from growing excessively.

claims.text: If overlapping readers always leave at least one reader active, no checkpoint can complete and the WAL can grow without bound.
claims.quote: However, if a database has many concurrent overlapping readers and there is always at least one active reader, then no checkpoints will be able to complete and hence the WAL file will grow without bound.

claims.text: Reader gaps can prevent starvation when checkpoints are attempted during times with no readers.
claims.quote: This scenario can be avoided by ensuring that there are "reader gaps": times when no processes are reading from the database and that checkpoints are attempted during those times.

claims.text: The WAL guide says RESTART and TRUNCATE checkpoints can block readers while running.
claims.quote: The disadvantage of using SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_RESTART and SQLITE_CHECKPOINT_TRUNCATE is that readers might block while the checkpoint is running.

claims.text: An active write transaction prevents mid-transaction WAL reset, so a large write can produce a large WAL.
claims.quote: A checkpoint can only complete when no other transactions are running, which means the WAL file cannot be reset in the middle of a write transaction. So a large change to a large database might result in a large WAL

claims.text: As of SQLite 3.11.0, a single transaction's WAL size should be proportional to the transaction, with changed pages written only once.
claims.quote: As of SQLite version 3.11.0 (2016-02-15), the WAL file for a single transaction should be proportional in size to the transaction itself. Pages that are changed by the transaction should only be written into the WAL file once.

claims.text: Older SQLite versions might write the same page into the WAL multiple times when a transaction exceeds the page cache.
claims.quote: However, with older versions of SQLite, the same page might be written into the WAL file multiple times if the transaction grows larger than the page cache.

c13: WAL activation, VFS shared-memory requirements, and network-filesystem limitation

The packet documents the SQLite 3.11.0 transaction WAL-size change but does not establish broader checkpoint history.
